title: Install Python, then verify the version you actually run
sources: Python 3.14 documentation: Using Python on Windows (Python install manager)
Python 3.14 documentation: Using Python on macOS
Python 3.14 documentation: Using Python on Unix platforms
Python 3.14 documentation: venv — creation of virtual environments
masterChecklist: Installing and selecting a Python version; CPython versus alternative implementations
Editor/IDE workflow, formatter, linter, debugger, terminal, and reading tracebacks
whyItMatters: Installing Python is only the first step. A terminal or editor may run a different interpreter, so a learner must verify which version is actually executing code.
simpleExplanation: Python is the language; CPython is the main interpreter distributed by the Python team. LearnVerse already has browser Python for practice, so installation is optional until you need local files, packages, or operating-system tools. On Windows, the current Python documentation recommends the Python install manager. On macOS, the Python team provides a signed installer package. On Linux, Python is commonly supplied by the distribution, and installation commands vary by distribution. Never replace an operating system's own Python casually. After any installation, open a NEW terminal and check the version and executable path. A project virtual environment is then made from the interpreter you chose; installing a package into one interpreter does not install it into every interpreter.
mentalModel: Installing is putting a kitchen in your house. Verifying the interpreter is checking which kitchen actually cooked today's meal.
outcomes: Follow the correct first-install path for Windows, macOS, or Linux without guessing a package-manager command.
Inspect the selected interpreter and version.
Know when the site browser runner is enough and when local Python is needed.

realWorldExample.scenario: A beginner installs Python and then sees `ModuleNotFoundError` in their editor even though a terminal package installation succeeded.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: Repeating package installation globally hides the fact that editor and terminal selected different interpreters.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Compare the interpreter path in each context, select the intended project environment, and install packages through that environment's interpreter.

workedExample.code:
import sys

print('implementation:', sys.implementation.name)
print('version:', f'{sys.version_info.major}.{sys.version_info.minor}')
print('browser runner:', sys.platform == 'emscripten')
print('executable is text:', isinstance(sys.executable, str))
explanation: The implementation line identifies CPython or another interpreter family.
The major/minor pair identifies the language release without assuming one fixed version.
The browser test distinguishes this site's Pyodide worker from a normal local interpreter.
sys.executable is a path or runtime representation of the current process; compare it across terminal and editor rather than assuming it names every installed Python.
workedExample.expectedOutput:
implementation: cpython
version: 3.14
browser runner: True
executable is text: True
workedExample.safeExperiment: In the LearnVerse runner print sys.executable; later run the same script locally and compare paths. Your local version number may differ from the bundled browser runtime.

procedure: Windows: if you only want to practise here, click Run Python and skip installing for now. For local work, open python.org/downloads in your own browser and obtain the Python install manager offered by the Python team; install it, then open a new PowerShell window.

Windows: run `py list` to inspect installed runtimes. If the required supported runtime is absent, use the manager's `py install <version>` command, for example `py install 3.14` when your project supports 3.14. Run `py -V:3.14 -V` and `py -V:3.14 -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"` to verify the selected interpreter. Do not assume `python` and `py` select the same version.

macOS: obtain the current supported macOS `.pkg` installer from python.org/downloads, check its version and compatibility on the installer page, complete the installer and its certificate-installation step when prompted, then open a new Terminal and run `python3 -V` and `python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"`. Do not delete Apple's Python.

Linux: first inspect `python3 -V` and `python3 -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"`. If a suitable interpreter is absent, use your distribution's official package instructions; exact package names and commands depend on the distribution. Do not overwrite its system Python just to follow a tutorial.
In the editor, select the verified interpreter. Run the worked example both in the editor and terminal and compare sys.executable.

For an isolated local project, run the chosen interpreter with `-m venv .venv`. On Windows PowerShell activate with `.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1`; on macOS/Linux bash or zsh use `source .venv/bin/activate`. You can also run the environment's interpreter by path without activation. Verify its sys.executable before installing project packages.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming installation succeeded because a download finished.
commonMistakes.why: The runtime may not have been installed or the current terminal may not see its commands.
commonMistakes.avoid: Open a fresh terminal and inspect version plus executable path.

commonMistakes.mistake: Installing packages into whichever `pip` appears first.
commonMistakes.why: That pip may belong to another interpreter.
commonMistakes.avoid: Run the selected interpreter with `-m pip` inside the project environment.

commonMistakes.mistake: Replacing an OS-managed Python to get a newer version.
commonMistakes.why: System tools may depend on the managed interpreter.
commonMistakes.avoid: Keep the system interpreter intact and use a separate supported runtime or virtual environment.

lab.title: Verify which Python runs your code
lab.safety: This in-site lab only inspects the bundled browser runtime. It does not install software or access your machine. Follow the written platform steps separately if you need local Python.
lab.starterCode:
import sys

def runtime_report():
    # Return implementation, major/minor version and whether this is browser Python.
    pass
guidedSteps: Return these values in a dictionary and click Run Tests.
If you install Python locally, run the same function there and compare the two reports.
checks: The report reflects the current process rather than hard-coded version numbers.
The browser worker is identified accurately.
hints: Browser Python in this site reports sys.platform == 'emscripten'.
lab.solutionExplanation: The function identifies only the process running it. Run it in two environments to compare them; it cannot list every installation on your computer.
lab.testCode:
r = runtime_report()
assert r['implementation'] == sys.implementation.name
assert r['version'] == (sys.version_info.major, sys.version_info.minor)
assert all(type(part) is int for part in r['version'])
assert r['browser'] is (sys.platform == 'emscripten')
print('PASS: current runtime identified')
challenges: Predict whether a virtual environment changes the interpreter path.
Find the error in hard-coding the version to 3.14 in the report.
After local setup, compare the editor's and terminal's sys.executable values.

simulation.prompt: A terminal and editor show different sys.executable values. What should you check first?
simulation.explanation: Different paths often mean different Python environments.

projectConnection.milestone: Record a verified interpreter and project environment in setup notes before adding dependencies.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: The learner can show matching terminal/editor interpreter paths and explain when the browser runner is sufficient.

assessment.question: Must you install Python before using LearnVerse's Run Python button?
assessment.explanation: The site already bundles a browser Python runtime.

assessment.question: Why inspect sys.executable after installation?
assessment.answer: It identifies the interpreter running this process.
assessment.explanation: Version commands alone can miss editor/terminal selection differences.

assessment.question: Should a Linux or macOS learner replace the OS-managed Python?
assessment.explanation: Keep system tooling intact and use a separate interpreter or project environment.
